1.Nf3 d5 2.c4.strategy: Challenges d5 from the flank before White commits a centre pawn, so the centre stays flexible and the bishops can be developed along the long diagonals. The cost is that Black may hold, take or advance past d5 and so decides how open the game becomes; White gets pressure on the centre from a distance instead of occupying it.

1.Nf3 d5 2.d4.strategy: Claims the centre at once and turns the game into a Queen's Pawn opening with the knight already developed. White keeps every plan open, from a quiet set-up to a fight for space, but gives up the independent character of 1.Nf3 and lets Black pick a standard defence. The move is entirely sound.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the kingside bishop and castle, for a compact system that is easy to repeat against most set-ups. White leaves the centre to Black at first and builds it up later, aiming for e4 and the space and attacking chances that come with it.

1.Nf3 d5 2.b3.name: Nimzowitsch–Larsen Attack
1.Nf3 d5 2.b3.background: Aron Nimzowitsch experimented with 1.b3 in the 1920s and 1930s but more commonly used the move order 1.Nf3 d5 2.b3. Bent Larsen played 1.b3 frequently from 1968 to 1972, and Bobby Fischer played it five times in 1970.
1.Nf3 d5 2.b3.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the queen's bishop, which together with the knight on f3 bears down on e5 and keeps Black from simply occupying it. White leaves the centre to Black for now.

1.Nf3 d5 2.e3.strategy: Opens the diagonal of the f1 bishop and aims for a solid, slow set-up in the centre. It shuts in the c1 bishop and commits White to that plan, so Black develops freely.

1.Nf3 d5 2.d3.name: Zukertort Opening: Old Indian Attack
1.Nf3 d5 2.d3.strategy: Prepares e4 for a reversed Old Indian set-up. It is flexible and sound, yet passive: Black takes the centre and can meet e4 on equal terms.

1.Nf3 d5 2.c3.strategy: Prepares d4 for a solid pawn structure, or e4 later. The pawn takes c3 from the b1 knight, which has to develop via d2, while Black develops freely.

1.Nf3 d5 2.Nc3.name: Zukertort Opening: Reversed Mexican Defence
1.Nf3 d5 2.Nc3.strategy: Develops a piece and prepares e4, but blocks the c-pawn, so the set-ups with c4 are no longer available. Black can gain space with ...d4 or simply develop and reach a comfortable position.

1.Nf3 d5 2.e4.strategy: Offers the e-pawn for quick piece play: after 2...dxe4 the knight jumps to g5, where it hits e4 and f7, and White hopes to win the pawn back or to break through on f7. Black can return the pawn or keep it and stands better either way, although an unprepared defender can fall into tactical traps.

1.Nf3 d5 2.a3.strategy: Prepares b4 and takes b4 from a bishop, but spends a tempo on a rim pawn while Black takes the centre.

1.Nf3 d5 2.a4.name: Zukertort Opening: The Potato
1.Nf3 d5 2.a4.strategy: Gains queenside space and stops ...b5, yet prepares nothing and weakens b4. Black develops and builds the centre without difficulty.

1.Nf3 d5 2.b4.name: Santasiere's Folly
1.Nf3 d5 2.b4.background: Named after the American master Anthony Santasiere (1904–1977), who originated and developed it and wrote a book about it, The Futuristic Chess Opening: Santasiere's Folly (Chess Digest, Dallas 1973).
1.Nf3 d5 2.b4.strategy: Gains queenside space with Bb2 in mind, but the b4-pawn has no pawn support and becomes a target. White spends time on the flank while Black develops freely.

1.Nf3 d5 2.h3.strategy: Takes g4 from Black's bishop before ...Bg4 is any threat, and spends a tempo that Black uses to claim the centre.

1.Nf3 d5 2.h4.strategy: Gains kingside space but does nothing for the centre or development, and loosens the kingside where White's king would castle. Black develops freely.

1.Nf3 d5 2.Na3.strategy: Develops the knight to the rim, from where it eyes b5 and c4, but it stands badly and blocks the a-pawn. Black takes the centre.

1.Nf3 d5 2.Rg1.name: Zukertort Opening: Ampel Variation
1.Nf3 d5 2.Rg1.strategy: Forfeits kingside castling to support a later g4, with nothing else ready to back the advance. White can only castle long or leave the king in the centre.

1.Nf3 d5 2.Ng5.strategy: Moves the knight a second time to hit f7 and h7, which the king and the rook defend. After 2...h6 it has to go back to f3 or h3, and Black has gained a tempo.

1.Nf3 d5 2.Nh4.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim with no defender, where a move of Black's e-pawn opens the queen's diagonal to h4. White must spend another tempo retreating it or covering it with g3.

1.Nf3 d5 2.Ne5.strategy: Moves the knight a second time to e5, where no pawn supports it. Black can offer a trade or drive it away with ...f6, gaining time, while White has developed nothing else.

1.Nf3 d5 2.Nd4.strategy: Centralises the knight with a second move, but ...e5 or ...c5 hits it at once and it must move again. Black builds a broad centre with gain of time.

1.Nf3 d5 2.Ng1.strategy: Returns the knight to its starting square and undoes the first move. White has made no progress, and Black has the extra tempo of d5 in hand.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g4.strategy: Loses a pawn at once: nothing defends g4, so 2...Bxg4 takes it, and White has only a half-open g-file to show for the weakened kingside.

1.Nf3 d5.name: Zukertort Opening
1.Nf3 d5.background: The usual reply in the 1920s, when Richard Réti began many of his games with 1.Nf3; against it he played 2.c4, the move order now named after him.

1.Nf3 d5 2.b3 Nf6.strategy: Develops the knight to its natural square, where it supports d5 and covers e4. Black commits to nothing yet, so every set-up with the bishops and the c- and e-pawns stays open, and White has to show what the b3 fianchetto is for.

1.Nf3 d5 2.b3 c5.background: Aron Nimzowitsch reached this position as White against Rudolf Spielmann at New York 1927 (3.Bb2 Nc6 4.e3 Nf6 5.Bb5) and won in 55 moves.
1.Nf3 d5 2.b3 c5.strategy: Fights for d4 from the flank before White can build a pawn centre, and prepares to bring out both knights. The game often becomes a reversed Nimzo-Indian, with Black's pawns on c5 and d5 facing White's fianchettoed bishop. The cost is that d5 has no pawn support until …e6, so Black has to watch that pawn while developing.

1.Nf3 d5 2.b3 Bg4.background: Raymond Keene, later the author of the book Nimzowitsch/Larsen Attack (1977), won as White against Vlatko Kovačević at Amsterdam 1973 after 2…Bg4 3.Bb2 Nd7.
1.Nf3 d5 2.b3 Bg4.strategy: Develops the bishop outside the pawn chain and puts pressure on the f3-knight, which guards e5 and d4. Taking on f3 removes that guard and may double White's pawns, but it gives up the bishop pair, and the bishop can be driven back by h3. Black develops quickly but may have to spend time on the bishop.

1.Nf3 d5 2.b3 Bf5.strategy: Develops the light-squared bishop outside the pawn chain before …e6 shuts it in, and eyes e4. Black aims for a solid reversed London set-up with …Nf6, …e6 and …c6 behind it. Development is easy, but White's plan is to force through e4 anyway, and the bishop can become a target.

1.Nf3 d5 2.b3 e6.strategy: Supports d5 and opens the f8-bishop, preparing quick kingside development and castling, usually reaching the same positions as 2…Nf6 with …e6. Sound, but it shuts in the c8-bishop before it can come out actively, giving up two of the main set-ups for no gain over 2…Nf6, while White builds freely.

1.Nf3 d5 2.b3 Nc6.strategy: Develops with pressure on d4 and e5 and prepares …e5, but it blocks the c-pawn and gives up the …c6 and …c5 set-ups. After 3.Bb2 an immediate …e5 loses a pawn to Nxe5 and Bxe5, so the advance needs more preparation first. Sound, yet the knight is committed before White has shown a plan.

1.Nf3 d5 2.b3 c6.strategy: Supports d5 with a pawn and keeps the c8-bishop free to come out in front of the pawn chain before …e6. Sound but passive: the pawn controls neither d4 nor e5, takes c6 from the b8-knight, and a later …c5 costs a second move, so White builds freely.

1.Nf3 d5 2.b3 b6.strategy: Mirrors White's set-up by preparing …Bb7, and leaves the centre to be settled later. The bishop on b7 looks at its own d5-pawn, so it does little until …c5 and …d4 or an exchange opens the diagonal, and White can build the centre meanwhile. Sound but unambitious.

1.Nf3 d5 2.b3 g6.strategy: Prepares …Bg7 to oppose Bb2 on the long diagonal. Sound but slow in the centre: the d5-pawn stands without pawn support, and White can hit it at once with c4.

1.Nf3 d5 2.b3 Nd7.strategy: Develops a piece and supports ...c5 and ...e5, which is sound against a quiet b3. But the knight blocks the c8-bishop, and ...e5 still loses a pawn to Nxe5 once the bishop stands on b2, so Black has less to show for the move than with ...Nf6.

1.Nf3 d5 2.b3 Na6.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, where it eyes b4 and c5 but does nothing for d4 or e5, which it would cover from c6. White builds the centre without opposition.

1.Nf3 d5 2.b3 Bd7.strategy: Develops the bishop, but to a passive square where it blocks the b8-knight's route to d7 instead of standing outside the pawn chain. Sound, since b3 makes no threat, but the bishop does little there and White builds the centre at leisure.

1.Nf3 d5 2.b3 Be6.strategy: Defends d5 with a piece, but the bishop blocks the e-pawn, so neither ...e6 nor ...e5 is available until it moves again. Sound against a quiet b3, yet it does less here than outside the pawn chain, and White builds at leisure.

1.Nf3 d5 2.b3 Qd7.strategy: Brings the queen out early, where it blocks the c8-bishop and the b8-knight's route to d7. Nothing is attacked, so White gains time while the queen stands in the way.

1.Nf3 d5 2.b3 Qd6.strategy: Brings the queen out early onto the a3–f8 diagonal, where 3.Ba3 attacks it at once, so it must move again or be shielded with …c5. No minor piece is developed meanwhile.

1.Nf3 d5 2.b3 Nh6.strategy: Heads for f5 by way of the rim, which is sound because nothing threatens the knight. But f6 is the natural square, where it would cover d5 and e4 at once, so the knight loses time on the way.

1.Nf3 d5 2.b3 a6.strategy: Sound, since b3 puts no pressure on Black, but it spends a tempo on a flank pawn without developing a piece or touching the centre. Its point is ...b5 and queenside space, which White can ignore while it builds up.

1.Nf3 d5 2.b3 a5.strategy: Gains queenside space with the idea of ...a4 against the b3-pawn. Sound at this stage, but it develops nothing, and the a-pawn no longer guards b6, so it costs a tempo for a plan White can ignore.

1.Nf3 d5 2.b3 b5.strategy: Advances a flank pawn without developing a piece, and the pawn on b5 has no defender: 3.e3 already threatens Bxb5+, and a4 can strike at it as well.

1.Nf3 d5 2.b3 f6.strategy: Prepares …e5, but takes f6 from the g8-knight and weakens e6 and the e8–h5 diagonal without developing a piece. White builds the centre freely.

1.Nf3 d5 2.b3 f5.strategy: Commits to a Stonewall-style pawn formation at once, which leaves e5 as a hole that Bb2 and a knight on e5 can exploit and delays the development of the kingside pieces.

1.Nf3 d5 2.b3 h6.strategy: Takes g5 away from White's knight, which is not threatening anything yet. Sound, because nothing punishes the slow move, but the tempo goes to the rim while White builds its position.

1.Nf3 d5 2.b3 h5.strategy: Starts a flank advance without developing a piece. Nothing punishes it yet, so it is sound, but it loosens the kingside for an attack that has no pieces behind it, and White takes the centre in the meantime.

1.Nf3 d5 2.b3 d4.strategy: Grabs space, but 3.Bb2 attacks the pawn twice, with bishop and knight, so Black must spend another move to hold it, and a later pawn move can undermine it. The pawn also no longer covers c4 and e4.

1.Nf3 d5 2.b3 Bh3.strategy: Loses the bishop at once to 3.gxh3, because no black piece can recapture on h3.

1.Nf3 d5 2.b3 Kd7.strategy: Forfeits castling and walks the king onto the d-file for no reason, where Ne5+ gives check at once. The king stays exposed in the centre and the h8-rook is left out of play.

1.Nf3 d5 2.b3 e5.strategy: Gives away the e-pawn: nothing guards e5, so 3.Nxe5 wins it, and the knight stands well in the centre.

1.Nf3 d5 2.b3 g5.strategy: Hangs the g-pawn to 3.Nxg5, since the e7-pawn blocks the queen's diagonal and no other piece guards it. The kingside is also loosened for nothing.

1.Nf3 d5 2.b3 c5 3.c4.strategy: Strikes at the d5 pawn from the flank, in the manner of an English Opening with b3 already played. If Black takes, White can regain the pawn with the b-pawn and open the b-file, or play on for quick development at a pawn's cost; if Black pushes the d-pawn instead, Black gains space but White gets targets to attack. Playable, but it gives Black the choice.

1.Nf3 d5 2.b3 c5 3.e4.name: Nimzowitsch–Larsen Attack: Norfolk Gambit
1.Nf3 d5 2.b3 c5 3.e4.strategy: A pawn gambit for activity: after ...dxe4 the f3-knight is attacked but jumps to e5, where it is strong, and White gets quick piece play. The compensation is real, but Black keeps an extra pawn and a strong centre, so White has to prove it.

1.Nf3 d5 2.b3 c5 3.Bb2.strategy: Puts the bishop on the long diagonal, the very reason for b3: it eyes the centre and the e5 square from a distance. White develops first and lets Black's pawns on d5 and c5 commit themselves, keeping the choice between a quiet build-up and a central break.

1.Nf3 d5 2.b3 c5 3.e3.strategy: A solid, flexible move: it opens the diagonal for the king's bishop and covers d4, so that ...d4 can be met by taking the pawn. White keeps the bishop move to b2 in hand and builds quietly. The cost is a slower grip on the long diagonal and none of Black's central pawns is challenged yet.

1.Nf3 d5 2.b3 c5 3.c4 dxc4.strategy: Black accepts the pawn and removes White's c-pawn from the fight for the centre. White can win it back at once with the b-pawn, opening the b-file, or leave it as a gambit for quicker development. The cost for Black is time: no piece is developed yet, so Black has to catch up while the lines open.

1.Nf3 d5 2.b3 c5 3.c4 Nf6.strategy: Develops a piece and adds to the control of d5 and e4, so that taking on d5 is met by a recapture with a developed knight in the centre. Black commits to nothing, keeps the d5 pawn firmly supported, and leaves White's c-pawn without a clear target.

1.Nf3 d5 2.b3 c5 3.c4 d4.strategy: Gains space and cramps White at once: the pawn on d4 takes the c3 and e3 squares away from White's pieces and shuts the long diagonal for the bishop that is about to arrive on b2. In return it needs support, and White can attack it with the knight, the bishop and a pawn break.

1.Nf3 d5 2.b3 c5 3.c4 dxc4 4.Nc3.name: Zukertort Opening: Regina-Nu Gambit
1.Nf3 d5 2.b3 c5 3.c4 dxc4 4.Nc3.strategy: Develops a piece instead of recovering the pawn, so White offers a real gambit. If Black takes on b3, the recapture with the a-pawn leaves White a pawn down with an open a-file and quick development as compensation. White has to prove that the lead in development is worth the pawn; offbeat.

1.Nf3 d5 2.b3 c5 3.c4 dxc4 4.bxc4.strategy: Recaptures at once with the b-pawn: material is level, White has a pawn on c4 again and the b-file opens for the rook. The price is an isolated a-pawn. Black gets a half-open d-file, but White's quicker development and the bishop coming to b2 keep the game balanced.

1.Nf3 d5 2.b3 c5 3.c4 dxc4 4.e3.strategy: Opens the bishop on f1 against the pawn on c4, which nothing of Black's defends, so White threatens to win the pawn back. Black can hold it with ...b5 or take on b3 and keep the extra pawn, and then White has to show that development is worth it. Playable, but less clear than the plain recapture.

1.Nf3 d5 2.e3 Nf6.strategy: Develops the knight to its best square, where it supports d5 and watches e4, and commits to no pawn structure. White's quiet e3 has not challenged the centre, so Black can build a comfortable position and choose the plan later.

1.Nf3 d5 2.e3 c5.strategy: Attacks the d4 square at once and claims space on the queenside, so White has no easy central pawn. The cost is that d5 loses the c-pawn's support and only the queen guards it, which invites White to challenge it immediately.

1.Nf3 d5 2.e3 Bf5.strategy: Develops the light-squared bishop outside the pawn chain before ...e6 shuts it in. White's quiet e3 has not claimed the centre, so Black can build its own pawn centre with the bishop active; Nh4 can harass it, but that puts the knight on the rim.

1.Nf3 d5 2.e3 c5 3.c4.strategy: Challenges d5 at once, while the c-pawn no longer supports it. The e3-pawn opens the f1-bishop's diagonal, so Black cannot win the pawn for free: a capture on c4 is met by the bishop taking it back.

1.Nf3 d5 2.e3 c5 3.d4.strategy: Strikes at the centre and challenges c5 at once, keeping the c-pawn back. If Black takes on d4 and White recaptures with the e-pawn, the centre opens and Black gets the half-open c-file against c2, so the game turns on development and piece play rather than on weaknesses.

1.Nf3 d5 2.e3 c5 3.b3.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the queen's bishop and holds back the d-pawn, so White does not claim the centre with pawns. A flexible but slow set-up: Black gets time to build its own centre, and White has to prove the bishop on b2 is worth the delay.

1.Nf3 d5 2.e3 c5 3.c4 dxc4.strategy: Takes the pawn, but only for the moment: the f1-bishop attacks c4 and nothing of Black's defends it, so White regains it with a developing move. Black resolves the central tension and gives White the easier, faster development.

1.Nf3 d5 2.e3 c5 3.c4 Nf6.strategy: Develops with a second defender of d5, so the pressure from the c-pawn leads only to an exchange: after cxd5 the knight recaptures and stands in the centre at once. Black keeps the c5-pawn as a lever against White's centre and gets an open, balanced game with easy development.

1.Nf3 d5 2.e3 c5 3.c4 e6.strategy: Backs up d5 with the e-pawn, so cxd5 is met by exd5 and Black keeps a pair of central pawns on c5 and d5. The price is the c8-bishop, shut in behind the e-pawn for now, and Black must soon decide how to meet a central pawn break by White.

1.Nf3 d5 2.e3 c5 3.c4 Nc6.strategy: Develops a piece and eyes d4, but leaves d5 with one defender less than it needs: cxd5 forces ...Qxd5, and Nc3 then attacks the queen and gains White a tempo. Black is not worse, but spends time on the queen while White develops.

1.Nf3 d5 2.e3 c5 3.c4 dxc4 4.b3.name: Zukertort Opening: Pachman Gambit
1.Nf3 d5 2.e3 c5 3.c4 dxc4 4.b3.strategy: A speculative gambit: instead of simply taking back on c4, White attacks the pawn a second time and plays for open lines against the queenside and a lead in development. If Black takes on b3, Black is a pawn up and White has to prove the compensation.

1.Nf3 d5 2.e3 c5 3.c4 dxc4 4.Bxc4.strategy: Regains the pawn at once with a developing move, the bishop eyeing f7. The pawns are level again, but Black has traded off its central d-pawn and is behind in development, so White has the freer game, with a central pawn break still to come against Black's c5-pawn.

1.Nf3 d5 2.e3 c5 3.c4 dxc4 4.Qa4+.strategy: Wins the pawn back with a check: if Black blocks with the knight it is pinned against the king, and if Black blocks with the bishop the queen simply takes c4. The cost is an early queen sortie, which Black can try to harass, but White regains the material with a lead in development.

1.Nf3 d5 2.e3 Nf6 3.c4.strategy: Challenges d5 with the c-pawn, using the quiet e3 to keep a solid structure behind it. White fights for the centre without committing the d-pawn, and a closed, positional game follows in which d4 is still available whenever White wants it.

1.Nf3 d5 2.e3 Nf6 3.d4.strategy: Takes the centre with the d-pawn at once and builds a compact pawn pair on d4 and e3, keeping the c-pawn back. A quiet, solid game follows in which White develops the bishop on d3 and plays for a central pawn break later.

1.Nf3 d5 2.e3 Nf6 3.b3.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the queen's bishop on the long diagonal and holds back both centre pawns. Sound and flexible, but slow: Black can take a broad share of the centre first, and White has to challenge it later with pieces and pawn breaks.

1.Nf3 d5 2.e3 Nf6 3.c4 e6.strategy: Backs up d5 with the e-pawn, a solid choice that opens the f8-bishop for castling. The cost is the c8-bishop, which is shut in behind the pawn, and freeing it is Black's long-term task in a slow, positional game.

1.Nf3 d5 2.e3 Nf6 3.c4 c6.strategy: Backs up d5 with the c-pawn, which keeps the c8-bishop's diagonal open and gives Black a sturdy, flexible centre. With White's e3 already played, the game is slow and closed, and Black can decide later whether to challenge White's centre or just develop.

1.Nf3 d5 2.e3 Nf6 3.c4 dxc4.strategy: Takes the pawn, which White regains at once with the f1-bishop, developing as it does. Black loosens the centre and spends a tempo on the capture, so White gets the more active pieces for a solid but slightly passive game for Black.

1.Nf3 d5 2.e3 Nf6 3.c4 e6 4.Nc3.strategy: Brings out the queenside knight to attack d5 a second time, so Black has to keep that pawn well guarded. White builds a classical set-up with c4 and e3 behind the pieces and keeps the d-pawn's advance in hand.

1.Nf3 d5 2.e3 Nf6 3.c4 e6 4.d4.strategy: Occupies the centre at once. With pawns on c4, d4 and e3 against d5 and e6, White has more space and Black a solid but cramped position, and White can still choose where the queenside knight goes.

1.Nf3 d5 2.e3 Nf6 3.c4 e6 4.b3.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the queen's bishop and keeps the d-pawn flexible. A sound but slower plan than taking the centre: it gives Black time to strike at White's pawns, and the bishop has to prove its worth on the long diagonal.

1.Nf3 d5 2.e3 Nf6 3.c4 e6 4.Nc3 Be7.strategy: Develops the bishop to a safe square behind the pawns and prepares castling, while d5 keeps its full support. Black does not need to hurry: the compact structure holds, and the one long-term worry is the c8-bishop behind e6.

1.Nf3 d5 2.e3 Nf6 3.c4 e6 4.Nc3 c5.strategy: Strikes at White's centre at once instead of waiting. After cxd5 and the recapture with the e-pawn, Black has a pair of hanging pawns on c5 and d5 and a free c8-bishop: active, open play against White's centre, with the pawns a target if the pieces do not support them.

1.Nf3 d5 2.e3 Nf6 3.c4 e6 4.Nc3 dxc4.strategy: Takes the pawn and lets White win it back with the f1-bishop at once, developing as it does. Black releases the pressure on d5 but loosens the centre and spends time on the capture, so White gets the easier development.

1.Nf3 d5 2.e3 Nf6 3.c4 e6 4.Nc3 Be7 5.d4.strategy: Occupies the centre at last and fixes the classical pawn structure, with pawns on c4, d4 and e3 against Black's d5 and e6. White has more space and the freer play; Black has a solid position and must find a way to free the c8-bishop.

1.Nf3 d5 2.e3 Nf6 3.c4 e6 4.Nc3 Be7 5.b3.strategy: Develops the c1-bishop to b2 without committing the d-pawn. It is slower than occupying the centre, and the bishop's diagonal is blocked for now by the knight on c3, so the set-up needs a later central pawn push to come alive.

1.Nf3 d5 2.e3 Nf6 3.c4 e6 4.Nc3 Be7 5.cx.strategy: Releases the tension in the centre. After the recapture with the e-pawn White has a half-open c-file against c7 and Black's c8-bishop is free, but White gives up the space advantage that the c-pawn was pressing for.
